title: The kings who couldn't lose
hookLine: kings who couldn't lift it decided to take Mithila instead
carry: ahamkara: the ego that can't bear to fail
last: BHUMI DEVI: THE EARTH IS A MOTHER.

lines: THE PRICE OF HER HAND: STRENGTH.
cards: Janaka made a decision about his daughter, and he announced it. Sita, he said, is viryashulka: the price of her hand is strength. Not gold, not alliances, not land.
Whoever can lift and string Shiva's bow may marry her. Word spread. Kings came from everywhere to try, and every one of them failed.
Then, Janaka tells Vishvamitra, something ugly happened. Wounded pride doesn't always go home quietly. Sometimes it comes back with an army.

teach.h: THE KINGS FAIL, AND BESIEGE MITHILA.
teach.b: The kings who failed were furious, insulted by a bow. They joined forces and laid siege to Mithila, and for a whole year the city was surrounded and supplies ran low. Janaka couldn't match their armies.
So he turned to austerity and prayer, and the gods answered him with an army of their own. The kings were scattered and fled.
Hindu teaching has a name for what drove those kings: ahamkara. Literally, the I-maker. It's the part of us that says: this is about me, my name, my standing.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces how a mind fixed on itself goes wrong, one step at a time.
Dwelling on something breeds clinging, clinging breeds wanting, wanting breeds anger, and anger clouds the mind. That's the siege, step by step.
The kings didn't really lose a bride; they lost face, and ahamkara can't bear that. Now look at Janaka.

No army, no way to win, and still he keeps his word: strength earns his daughter, not force. He sets down his own pride and turns to the gods. That's the spirit behind a small ritual you'll see at temples.

teach.h: THE COCONUT: A SHELL CRACKED OPEN.
teach.b: Many Hindus break a coconut before God, and families often explain it this way: the hard shell is the ego, cracked open so what's sweet inside can be offered.
So when Janaka finally shows Rama the bow, it's no party trick. It arrives in an iron chest on an eight-wheeled cart, hauled in, the text says, by five thousand strong men.
The whole hall waits to see what the young prince will do.

how: Across India, the contest of the bow is staged in Ramlila performances; later retellings such as the Ramcharitmanas present it as a swayamvara, while Valmiki describes Sita as viryashulka, won by strength.

o: a weapon the gods gave the kings to besiege Mithila
the test of strength set for whoever would marry Sita
a bow Janaka paid for with Mithila's treasury

games.q: the test and its cost — tap the pairs.
p: the I-maker: this is about me

s: the failed kings went home quietly
their wounded pride turned into a year-long siege of Mithila.
in the Gita, anger grows out of clinging and wanting
dwelling breeds clinging, clinging breeds wanting, wanting breeds anger, and anger clouds the mind.
Janaka set Sita's bride-price in gold
he set it in strength: viryashulka.

games.q: you're Janaka. kings have failed your test and now surround your city. what do you do?
o: give Sita to the strongest of them.
turn to austerity and prayer, and keep your word.
break the bow so no one can try.
games.why: he sets aside his pride, not his promise, and turns to tapas; the gods give him an army, and the kings are scattered.

practice: Remember a time something didn't go your way in front of others, and feel where the sting lands. That's ahamkara, the I-maker. Don't fight it.
On each breath out, picture it as a hard shell cracking a little, like a coconut offered at a temple. If you pray, offer the sting to God. If you don't, let the memory sit there, smaller.

wordCard.voice: Janaka's bow. The bow no king could lift, set as the price of Sita's hand. Failing to lift it sent proud kings to besiege Mithila for a year.

orig.note: Sanskrit ahaṃkāra: aham, I, plus kāra, maker. the sense of 'me' that takes everything personally.

carryVoice: Your line: ahamkara, the ego that can't bear to fail. The kings had armies; Janaka had his word. See you tomorrow.
